newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to cut farm subsidies in WTO entry strategy.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to cut farm subsidies in WTO entry strategy.

text.p: Taiwan plans to streamline its agricultural subsidy system to improve its chances of gaining entry to the World Trade Organisation (WTO), officials of the cabinet-level Council of Agriculture said on Monday.
The measures will likely result in Taiwan farmers cutting back their production of -- or even abandoning -- many crops as unprofitable, the officials added.

Taiwan plans to scrap its current system of specific subsidies for each type of crop in favor of a practise allowed by the WTO of calculating subsidies based on the amount of land being cultivated, said council official Liao An-ding.
Liao spoke by telephone as Taiwanese and U.S. negotiators discussed the island's WTO entry bid in Taipei.
Under the new system, certain crops that require heavy subsidisation would no longer be profitable for local farmers to grow and Taiwan would be forced to increase imports of those items, Liao said.
Liao said the new policy was aimed mainly at satisfying U.S. concerns as Washington wields major influence in WTO membership decisions.
"Taiwan has little power to negotiate and can only try hard to meet U.S. demands on various issues," Liao said.
Local media have reported that agricultural subsidies were central to Monday's agenda at the closed-door U.S.-Taiwan talks on Taiwan's WTO application, being held all this week in Taipei.
U.S. and Taiwan officials declined to comment on the outcome of the talks.
Another Council of Agriculture official, Ku Te-yeh, said the agency expected that domestic production of many types of grain would die out under the subsidy reforms.

The council estimates Taiwan rice production will drop by eight percent and sugar cane by 15.8 percent in six years as a result of the reforms, Ku said. He said production of feed corn is also likely to be hit.

The island grows and consumes about 1.8 million tonnes of rice a year and has stores of more than 700,000 tonnes. Taiwan does not import rice and -- like Japan -- has long regarded rice self-sufficiency a matter of national security and pride.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join the WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade (GATT), as a customs territory under the name of Chinese Taipei.
GATT was replaced by the WTO in January 1995.
Taiwan has made major concessions in recent years in a bid to join the world trade body, allowing more imports and opening up domestic markets and even state monopolies.
But China, which regards Taiwan as a renegade province since a civil war split them in 1949, has said it would only accept Taiwan's WTO membership after China itself is allowed entry.

The United States, Europe, Japan and Canada have steadfastly blocked China's membership on grounds that the communist giant's economy is unfairly protected from imports and that its trading system is insufficiently transparent.
